title: Pretraining vs Fine-tuning
summary: Modern LLMs are built in stages: expensive pretraining on huge text corpora gives general knowledge, then fine-tuning adapts the model to specific tasks or behaviors. Instruction tuning and RLHF make models helpful and safe. Knowing this pipeline hel
content:
# Pretraining vs Fine-tuning ##### ₹18 lakh spent solving the wrong problem A logistics startup in Gurugram wanted an assistant that could answer questions about their internal shipping policies. Their CTO's instinct was fine-tuning: take an open 7B model, train it on their policy documents, ship it. Six weeks and roughly ₹18 lakh in GPU time later, they had a model that spoke fluently about shipping policy and got the details wrong about a third of the time. Worse, when a policy changed in March, the model still confidently cited the old one — because the old one was baked into its weights. They rebuilt it as RAG in nine days. Retrieve the relevant policy paragraph, put it in the prompt, let a stock model read and answer. Accuracy went to 94%, policy updates took effect the moment someone edited a document, and the monthly cost was under ₹20,000. The mistake was not technical incompetence. It was a category error: **they used fine-tuning to inject knowledge, when fine-tuning teaches behaviour and retrieval supplies knowledge.** Understanding how models are built — what each training stage actually does — is what lets you make that call correctly. That is today. ##### The three-stage pipeline Every modern assistant model goes through roughly the same sequence. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Raw internet text
trillions of tokens"] --> B["STAGE 1: Pretraining
next-token prediction
weeks, ₹10-1000 crore"] B --> C["Base model
knows language & facts
but only completes text"] C --> D["STAGE 2: Instruction tuning (SFT)
10K-1M prompt/response pairs
hours-days, ₹1-50 lakh"] D --> E["Instruct model
follows instructions"] E --> F["STAGE 3: Preference tuning
RLHF / DPO
days, ₹5-100 lakh"] F --> G["Aligned assistant
helpful, harmless, honest"] C -.you can start here.-> H["Your fine-tune
or prompting"] E -.usually start here.-> H G -.usually start here.-> H ``` Each stage costs orders of magnitude less than the one before, and each changes something different about the model. ##### Stage 1: Pretraining The objective is Day 24's: predict the next token. That is all. What makes it work is scale. Llama 3 was trained on over 15 trillion tokens. GPT-4's training cost is estimated in the hundreds of crores of rupees. The data is filtered web crawl, books, code, Wikipedia, and academic papers. **What pretraining produces:** a model that has absorbed grammar, facts, reasoning patterns, code syntax, and multiple languages — because predicting internet text well requires all of it. **What it does not produce:** an assistant. A base model given "What is the capital of Maharashtra?" might reply: ``` What is the capital of Maharashtra? What is the capital of Gujarat? What is the capital of Karnataka? ``` It is not being unhelpful. It is doing exactly what it was trained to do — continuing a document that looks like a list of quiz questions. That is the most likely continuation on the internet. **You will almost certainly never pretrain a model.** The knowledge matters because it explains what a base model is and is not, and why the next two stages exist. Related terms worth pinning down: - **Self-supervised** — labels come from the data itself (the next token), so no human annotation is needed. This is what makes trillion-token training possible. - **Foundation model** — a large pretrained model intended as a base for many downstream tasks. GPT-4, Llama 3, Claude, Mistral. - **Emergent capabilities** — abilities that appear at scale without being targeted, as Day 24 covered. ##### Stage 2: Instruction tuning Also called supervised fine-tuning (SFT). Take the base model and train it on curated (instruction, response) pairs. ```json {"instruction": "Summarise this support ticket in one sentence.", "input": "Customer reports UPI payment debited but order not confirmed...", "output": "A customer's UPI payment was debited without order confirmation."} ``` Typically 10,000 to 1,000,000 examples, written or curated by humans. The objective is still next-token prediction — but now on text that *demonstrates the behaviour you want*. The change is dramatic and surprisingly cheap. The Alpaca project famously instruction-tuned Llama-7B on 52,000 examples generated by GPT-3.5, for about ₹50,000, and got a model that behaved recognisably like an assistant. **Instruction tuning changes behaviour, not knowledge.** After SFT, the model answers questions instead of continuing them. It has not learned new facts. That distinction is the Gurugram lesson, stated precisely. ##### Stage 3: RLHF Instruction tuning gets you a model that follows instructions. It does not get you one that follows them *well* — helpfully, safely, at the right length, refusing when it should. The problem is that "good response" is easy to recognise and hard to specify. You cannot write a loss function for helpfulness. But humans can compare two responses and say which is better. RLHF (Christiano et al., 2017; applied to LLMs in InstructGPT, Ouyang et al., 2022) turns that comparison into a training signal. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["SFT model"] --> B["Generate 2-4 responses
per prompt"] B --> C["Humans rank them
best to worst"] C --> D["Train a REWARD MODEL
to predict human preference"] D --> E["Optimise the LLM with PPO
to maximise reward"] E --> F["KL penalty keeps it close
to the SFT model"] F --> G["Aligned model"] E -.without KL penalty.-> H["Reward hacking:
gibberish that scores high"] ``` Three steps: 1. **Collect preferences.** Show humans several model responses to the same prompt; they rank them. 2. **Train a reward model.** A separate network that takes (prompt, response) and outputs a scalar score, trained to match human rankings. 3. **Optimise with RL.** Use PPO to update the LLM to produce responses the reward model scores highly — with a KL-divergence penalty preventing it from drifting too far from the SFT model. **The KL penalty is essential.** Without it, the model discovers adversarial outputs that fool the reward model while being useless to humans — reward hacking. It might learn that longer responses score higher and start padding everything, or find bizarre phrasings the reward model over-rates. **The headline result from InstructGPT:** a 1.3B parameter RLHF model was *preferred by human evaluators* over the 175B base GPT-3. Alignment beat 100× the parameter count. That finding is why every serious assistant model now goes through this stage. **DPO** (Direct Preference Optimization, Rafailov et al., 2023) has largely replaced PPO in practice. It achieves similar results by optimising directly on preference pairs with a clever loss, skipping the separate reward model and the RL loop entirely. It is far simpler to implement and much more stable. If you are doing preference tuning today, start with DPO. ##### Base vs instruct vs chat You will see all three on the Hugging Face Hub, and picking wrong wastes days. | | Base | Instruct | Chat / RLHF | |---|---|---|---| | Example | `Llama-3-8B` | `Llama-3-8B-Instruct` | `Llama-3-8B-Instruct` (RLHF'd) | | Trained on | Raw text | Instruction pairs | + human preferences | | Behaviour | Completes text | Follows instructions | Helpful, safe, conversational | | Needs a chat template | No | **Yes** | **Yes** | | Use for | Further pretraining, your own SFT | Task-specific fine-tuning | Direct deployment | **The chat template is a real gotcha.** Instruct models expect a specific format with role markers, and using the wrong one degrades output badly: ```python from transformers import AutoTokenizer tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct") messages = [ {"role": "system", "content": "You are a concise logistics assistant."}, {"role": "user", "content": "What is our standard delivery SLA for Pune?"}, ] prompt = tok.apply_chat_template(messages, tokenize=False, add_generation_prompt=True) print(prompt) ``` Use `apply_chat_template` rather than hand-building the string. Every model family formats differently, and the tokenizer knows its own format. ##### The decision: prompt, RAG, or fine-tune? This is the question you will actually be asked in interviews and in planning meetings. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["What do you need?"] --> B{"Model lacks
KNOWLEDGE
or BEHAVIOUR?"} B -->|Knowledge:
facts, docs, data| C{"Does it change?"} C -->|Yes, frequently| D["RAG
retrieve at query time"] C -->|Rarely, and it's huge| E["RAG still, usually.
Fine-tune only if latency
or cost demands it"] B -->|Behaviour:
format, tone, style, task| F{"Can prompting
get you there?"} F -->|Yes| G["PROMPT ENGINEERING
cheapest, fastest, reversible"] F -->|No, after real effort| H{"Have 500+ good
examples?"} H -->|Yes| I["FINE-TUNE
LoRA/QLoRA"] H -->|No| J["Collect examples first,
use few-shot meanwhile"] ``` | | Prompting | RAG | Fine-tuning | |---|---|---|---| | **Adds** | Instructions, examples | External knowledge | Behaviour, style, format | | **Cost** | ₹0 setup | Moderate | High | | **Time** | Minutes | Days | Weeks | | **Update knowledge** | Edit prompt | Edit documents | Retrain | | **Citations possible** | No | **Yes** | No | | **Reduces hallucination** | Slightly | **Substantially** | No | | **Latency** | Baseline | +retrieval | Baseline or better | | **Needs data** | 0–10 examples | Documents | 500+ examples | **The rules that follow from this table:** 1. **Always try prompting first.** It is free, instant, and reversible. A surprising fraction of problems dissolve with a better prompt. 2. **Use RAG for knowledge.** Facts, documents, anything that changes, anything you need to cite. This is the Gurugram fix. 3. **Fine-tune for behaviour.** A consistent output format, a specific tone, a narrow task the model does clumsily, or matching a JSON schema reliably. 4. **They compose.** A fine-tuned model with RAG and a good prompt is the strongest configuration, and most production systems use all three. A legitimate fourth reason to fine-tune: **cost and latency.** A fine-tuned 3B model can match a prompted 70B model on a narrow task, at a fraction of the inference cost. If you are serving millions of requests, that arithmetic dominates. ##### What fine-tuning cannot do Worth stating explicitly, because the misconception is expensive: - **It does not reliably add facts.** Training on documents teaches the model to *sound like* those documents, not to recall them accurately. It will confidently produce plausible-but-wrong details. - **It does not make knowledge updatable.** Baked into weights means retraining to change. - **It does not provide citations.** You cannot trace an answer to a source. - **It can cause catastrophic forgetting.** Aggressive fine-tuning degrades general capability. - **It does not fix a badly-specified task.** If you cannot describe what you want in a prompt, you probably cannot describe it in training data either. ##### Common mistakes - **Fine-tuning to inject knowledge** instead of using RAG — the ₹18 lakh error. - **Using a base model and expecting instruction-following.** - **Using an instruct model without its chat template.** - **Skipping prompt engineering** and jumping to fine-tuning. - **Fine-tuning on 50 examples** and getting overfitting rather than learning. - **Full fine-tuning when LoRA would do** — tomorrow's topic. - **Assuming RLHF makes a model truthful.** It makes it *preferred by raters*, which correlates with but is not identical to correct. - **Not realising RLHF introduces its own biases** — sycophancy and excessive hedging are known side effects of optimising for human approval. - **Fine-tuning without a held-out evaluation set**, so you cannot tell whether it helped. - **Ignoring the base model's license** before building a product on a fine-tune of it. ##### Hands-on: make the decision explicit Your practical task is a decision flowchart for prompting versus fine-tuning versus RAG. Build it as a Mermaid diagram in your notes, then — this is the valuable part — run five real business problems through it and write down the answer and the reasoning for each. Try: "answer questions about our HR policy," "always return valid JSON matching this schema," "write in our brand voice," "classify support tickets into 40 internal categories," "explain our product to customers in Marathi." Two of those want RAG, two want fine-tuning, and one wants a better prompt. Working out which is the skill. The mini project compares three real models — a base, an instruction-tuned, and an RLHF'd one. Use `gpt2` (base), `google/flan-t5-base` (instruction-tuned), and any chat model you can access. Give all three the identical prompt, ideally something like "Explain photosynthesis to a class 8 student." The base model will continue rather than answer, the instruct model will answer, and the chat model will answer well and appropriately pitched. Put the three outputs side by side in your report — that comparison is more convincing than any explanation. The assignment summarises RLHF in under 500 words. Structure it as the three steps, then explain the KL penalty and why it is needed, then close with the InstructGPT result that 1.3B RLHF beat 175B base. Mention DPO as the modern simplification. Keep it tight — the word limit is deliberate, and being able to explain RLHF concisely is exactly what an interviewer is testing. ##### Key takeaways - **Three stages build a modern assistant**: pretraining gives knowledge and language, instruction tuning gives instruction-following, and RLHF/DPO gives helpfulness — each costing orders of magnitude less than the last. - **A base model completes text; it does not answer questions.** That is not a defect, it is exactly what next-token prediction produces. - **Fine-tuning teaches behaviour, RAG supplies knowledge.** Confusing the two is the most expensive mistake in applied GenAI. - **Always try prompting first**, then RAG, then fine-tuning — in increasing order of cost, time, and irreversibility. - **RLHF's headline result — a 1.3B aligned model beating 175B unaligned — shows alignment can matter more than scale**, and DPO now achieves it without the RL machinery.
practical_task_reference: Create a decision flowchart for when to use prompting, fine-tuning, or RAG for a given business problem.
